title: Under the Desert Sky, Counting What I Cannot Count
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] We'd driven three hours out of the city specifically to escape its glow, and even so, I hadn't quite prepared myself for what greeted us once we stopped.
Narrator: The moment I stepped out of the car, the sky simply overwhelmed me, thick with stars in a way I'd genuinely never witnessed before.
Narrator: [carefully] I'd grown up assuming the sky held maybe a few hundred visible stars, based on whatever faint scattering the city allowed through its haze of light.
Narrator: Out there, it held thousands, layered so densely in places that the darkness between them seemed almost incidental, a mere backdrop for something far larger.
Narrator: [reflective] I lay back against the still-warm sand and tried, absurdly, to count them, as though counting could somehow make the scale feel more manageable.
Narrator: I gave up almost immediately, obviously, yet the attempt itself left me strangely humbled, aware of how small my usual concerns suddenly felt.
Narrator: [honestly] My uncle, who'd guided desert treks for over twenty years, told me the Bedouin used to navigate entire journeys by these same stars, trusting patterns rather than instruments.
Narrator: I asked him whether he ever grew used to this view, whether repetition eventually dulled it the way most things dull with familiarity.
Narrator: [gently] He said the opposite happens, if anything. The more he understood about the stars' distances and ages, the more staggering the whole display became to him.
Narrator: Something about that struck me deeply, that knowledge here didn't diminish wonder, it deepened it, layer upon layer, the more he learned.
Narrator: [calmly] I thought about how rarely I actually look up in ordinary life, how easily a ceiling of light pollution convinces us that this, the sliver we see, is the whole sky.
Narrator: Driving home before dawn, I kept glancing at the rearview mirror, as though something that vast could somehow be left behind so easily.
